title: 5 Best ChatGPT Prompts for SQL Queries (2026)
description: From question to trustworthy query: schema-aware drafting, correctness checks, performance tuning, and turning one-off SQL into reusable views.

steps.title: Teach it your schema once
steps.promptText:
Here is my database schema:
[PASTE CREATE TABLE STATEMENTS OR COLUMN LISTS]

Database: [POSTGRES/MYSQL/SQLITE/BIGQUERY]. Confirm your understanding: list each table's purpose in one line, the join keys between them, and any columns whose names are ambiguous (tell me what you're assuming they mean). Ask me up to 3 clarifying questions if the schema leaves real ambiguity.
steps.whyThisTool: One schema-grounding step makes every later query dramatically more accurate.
steps.outputExpected: A one-line-per-table summary and explicit assumptions you can correct now, not after a wrong query.

steps.title: Draft the query from the business question
steps.promptText:
Using that schema, write a query answering: [BUSINESS QUESTION — e.g. "monthly revenue per plan for the last 6 months, excluding refunded orders"].

Rules: comment each non-obvious clause with WHY, state which rows get excluded and by which condition, and if the question is ambiguous, implement the most likely reading and note the alternative.
steps.whyThisTool: Forcing the exclusions to be explicit is where most 'wrong number in the dashboard' bugs die.
steps.outputExpected: A commented query plus a one-line statement of what's excluded and why.

steps.title: Verify correctness with adversarial rows
steps.promptText: Invent 8-10 rows of sample data that include the tricky cases for this query: refunds, nulls, timezone-boundary timestamps, duplicate events, a user with zero orders. Show the table, trace the query against it by hand, and confirm the output matches the business intent. If it doesn't, fix the query and re-trace.
steps.whyThisTool: Hand-tracing adversarial rows catches the NULL and boundary bugs that look fine in production until month-end.
steps.outputExpected: A worked example proving the query right — or a fixed query.

steps.title: Performance pass
steps.promptText: Assume the big tables here have [ROUGH ROW COUNTS]. Analyze this query's plan risks: full scans, join order, functions on indexed columns, and OR conditions blocking index use. Suggest specific indexes (with exact CREATE INDEX statements) and a rewritten query if it materially helps. State the trade-off of each index.
steps.whyThisTool: Index suggestions with explicit trade-offs beat 'add an index' hand-waving.
steps.outputExpected: Concrete CREATE INDEX statements and an honest cost note for each.

steps.title: Make it reusable
steps.promptText: This query will be needed regularly. Convert it into [A VIEW / CTE LIBRARY / dbt MODEL], parameterized by [DATE RANGE / SEGMENT]. Add a header comment documenting: business definition, exclusions, owner, and the verification date. Suggest a name that says what it MEANS, not what it joins.
steps.whyThisTool: One-off queries become tribal knowledge; named, documented views become infrastructure.
steps.outputExpected: A paste-ready view/model with a documentation header your future teammates will thank you for.

faq.q: Does this work for BigQuery / Snowflake?
faq.a: Yes — name your dialect in step 1 and syntax adapts. The correctness and performance steps matter even more at warehouse scale.

faq.q: Can I trust AI-generated SQL in production?
faq.a: Trust the process, not the first draft: step 3's adversarial-row trace is the gate. A query that survives it is safer than most hand-written SQL that never got one.

faq.q: Why is Gemini tagged on this pack?
faq.a: For BigQuery-heavy stacks, Gemini's grounding in Google's dialect is convenient. The prompts run unchanged in either tool.

benefit: Queries you can trust in production — verified against the rows that usually break them.
